headline: Bangladesh faces Afghanistan in historic red-ball Test in UAE
summary: Bangladesh will play a one-off Test against Afghanistan today, marking their first red-ball match in the UAE. This non-World Test Championship fixture offers the Tigers a crucial opportunity to hone their skills.
details: Bangladesh is set to play a one-off Test match against Afghanistan today, Friday, October 9. The historic red-ball encounter will commence at 12 PM Bangladesh time at the Sheikh Zayed Cricket Stadium in Abu Dhabi, UAE. This marks the first time the Tigers will compete in a red-ball format on Emirati soil.

The two teams have previously met in two Test matches, with each side securing one victory. In 2019, Bangladesh suffered a 224-run defeat in Chattogram, but they avenged it with a massive 546-run win in Mirpur in 2023.

In their limited Test history, Najmul Hossain Shanto leads with the bat, scoring 270 runs with two centuries in just two innings. Rashid Khan tops the bowling charts, having claimed 11 wickets in two innings.

The Abu Dhabi pitch has seen varied Test performances, including a record high of 598 runs in an innings, but also a low of 72 runs where a strong team like England was bowled out. This indicates a potentially unpredictable surface.

While this match is not part of the World Test Championship, it serves as a vital chance for the Tigers to fine-tune their performance. It follows their recent historic success against Australia, providing momentum for this challenge.

headline: Dengue vaccine now available in Australia, but Bangladesh, facing severe outbreak, awaits
summary: While Australia approves and offers the effective Qdenga dengue vaccine to its citizens, Bangladesh continues to battle a severe dengue outbreak with thousands infected and many deaths, prompting calls for vaccine availability.
details: Eight-year-old Rumaisa tragically passed away from dengue at Square Hospital in Dhaka on October 1. The third-grader developed a fever on September 29, and despite no severe prior symptoms, her condition rapidly deteriorated within three days.

On the morning of October 1, Rumaisa was eating and playing normally, with no rashes or visible bleeding and a platelet count of 140,000. However, she suddenly experienced convulsions and seizures at noon, leading to internal bleeding just an hour after being admitted to the PICU.

Her parents, both doctors—her father an ICU specialist and her mother an ophthalmologist—were unable to save their child from the sudden onset of severe dengue. This tragic event deeply affected family friends, including the author, highlighting the helplessness even medical professionals face.

Amidst this grief, a ray of hope emerged from Sydney: the effective dengue vaccine ‘Qdenga’ by Japanese manufacturer Takeda became available to the public in Australia. Anyone aged four or older can receive two doses with a GP's prescription.

Australia has virtually no local dengue transmission, with nearly 100% of its annual 2,500 cases being travel-related. Despite this low domestic risk, the Australian government approved the vaccine for proactive citizen protection, offering relief to expatriate Bangladeshis planning visits home.

This stark contrast highlights a critical issue: the vaccine is readily available where the risk is minimal, yet absent in Bangladesh, where dengue claims lives daily. This disparity prompted the author to write about the urgent need for the vaccine in high-risk areas.

Bangladesh continues to face an unrelenting wave of dengue infections and deaths, with September alone seeing numerous fatalities and thousands of new cases. Each death represents a family devastated, like nine-year-old Arfa, who lost her mother at three days old and now her father to dengue.

Local government bodies, primarily responsible for mosquito control, are largely inactive despite having nearly 48,000 committees from union to national levels. This administrative failure exacts a heavy toll, particularly on children, who are disproportionately affected by the disease.

While mosquito control and improved pediatric ICU facilities are crucial, the Qdenga vaccine's scientific efficacy is proven, showing over 80% effectiveness against confirmed dengue and reducing hospitalization risk by 95% in trials. The WHO's SAGE group recommended it for 6-16 year olds in high-transmission areas in October 2023, and it received prequalification in May 2024.

Over forty countries, including neighboring India, have already approved Qdenga for ages 4-60. However, despite global progress, Bangladesh has yet to provide a clear message regarding the registration or policy decision for Qdenga, leaving its citizens vulnerable.
